headline: A Radio Call at 0400 and a Swordfish Off Oceanographer
subhead: The daytime drop is paying off on the eastern grounds, and the fleet that gambled on fuel this week came home with fish to show for it.
body_markdown:
The VHF chatter out of Montauk this week had a different tone to it — less small talk, more numbers. A boat working the daytime drop off Oceanographer Canyon called in a swordfish on the deck before most of the coffee at the dock had gone cold, and by midmorning two more boats had checked in with yellowfin and at least one bigeye. That's the kind of radio traffic that gets captains checking fuel tanks a little more carefully before they commit to the run.

We flagged this last week — said the east canyons were the zone most likely to produce a genuine surprise if the swordfish pattern held. It held. The live squid drop during daylight hours off Oceanographer has turned from a curiosity into a repeatable program, and it's the kind of thing that changes how a trip gets planned. Instead of running out at 2 a.m. to be on the tuna grounds by first light and grinding bait all day, boats are stretching the day — working the swordfish drop through the heat of the afternoon when the tuna bite typically goes quiet, then picking up green stick fish or a mackerel bait on the troll in the last couple hours of light on the way in.

The tactics haven't changed much, they've just been dialed in. Live-lined mackerel, either flat-lined off the corner or fished under a balloon, has been drawing yellowfin up out of the temperature breaks along the edge, particularly where the color goes from that dirty green inshore water to the cleaner blue past the shelf. Green stick trolling with rigged ballyhoo has been the more efficient way to cover water when the fish are scattered rather than balled up, and it's been putting bigeye and yellowfin in the box on the troll before the boats even set up to drift bait. The swordfish program is simpler than people think but not easy — a whole squid or a rigged strip bait fished on the bottom or just off it during daylight, patience while the current does its work, and a captain willing to sit on a spot for hours instead of moving every twenty minutes. That patience has been the difference this week between boats that connected and boats that didn't.

This is a fishery that runs on fuel math, and there's no getting around it. From Montauk, Block Island, or the Rhode Island ports, a trip to Oceanographer or Hydrographer is an all-day commitment before a hook ever gets wet — long enough that the boats making the run are doing it with a plan, not a whim. Nobody's running out there on a maybe. The captains who went this week did it because the radio chatter and the pattern justified the diesel, and it paid for itself. That's the calculation every trip out here comes down to: is the bite worth the burn. Right now, for the boats willing to make the commitment to Oceanographer specifically, the answer's been yes.

Veatch and Atlantis haven't produced the same volume of radio traffic this week — that doesn't mean they're empty, it means the fleet's attention and the fish have both been concentrated closer to Oceanographer for now. Hydrographer got a mention or two but nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet. When a bite like this settles into one canyon, it often takes a few more days before boats start testing the neighbors, and that's usually how you find out if it's a real spread of fish or just a hot pocket.

Conditions have been stable enough to keep this going — no big blow pushing through, no hard cold front yet to shake up the water. That stability is exactly what's let the swordfish pattern mature instead of getting interrupted before it had a chance to prove itself. The tuna have stayed put on the temperature breaks rather than sliding around chasing a moving edge, which is why the same general area has kept producing day after day instead of forcing boats to hunt.

Looking at the next several days, the smart play is the same one that's been working: run for Oceanographer if the weather window allows it, work the troll and live bait through the morning for yellowfin and bigeye, then transition into the daytime swordfish drop through the afternoon rather than running home early. Boats with the range and the patience to fish a full day out there have been the ones cashing in, not the ones making a hit-and-run trip. If the pattern holds through the week — and there's no signal yet that it's breaking down — Hydrographer and Veatch are worth a look for any boat willing to scout on the way past, since a stable bite like this one tends to bleed sideways into the neighboring grounds eventually.

The one thing to watch is the calendar. Late September is when the first real cold fronts start lining up, and when one comes through hard it tends to tighten these offshore bites down toward the true canyon edges fast. Nothing in the pattern says that's imminent, but any captain who's run this water long enough builds in a buffer day. For now, the fuel math still favors the run, and the radio's still worth listening to before first light.
